items.title: Copper, not the yuan, is now the cleanest read on China's economy
items.idea: The old China boom poured copper into apartments and roads. The new industrial cycle pours it into electricity grids, data centers, EVs and AI infrastructure. Dark Side of the Boom argues copper is now a cleaner signal for AUD than USD/CNY or Chinese equities, because it captures the electrification and AI-capex cycle specifically rather than a stimulus bet.
items.angle: This is a structural regime change for AUD trades — not a China-GDP bet anymore, but an AI-capex bet in disguise.
items.tweetA: Everyone still trades AUD as a China-GDP proxy. It isn't one anymore — property's dead, but copper demand from grids, EVs and AI data centers is the new driver. You're not betting on Chinese consumers, you're betting on the global AI buildout with extra steps.
items.tweetB: If AUD is now a copper-into-AI-capex trade instead of a China-stimulus trade, it should start correlating more with $CPER and the Philly Semi index than with CNH. Nobody's back-tested that correlation shift yet.

charts.desc: No chart in email; article may include FX/copper charts — worth opening.

items.title: The Fed isn't hiking — it's outsourcing the hike to the bond market
items.idea: Citadel's Nohshad Shah flags the contradiction at the center of the Warsh Fed: hawkish rhetoric, no soft target, yet no hike, leaning on the fact that markets already tightened via higher long-end yields. But a long-end selloff driven by term premium and eroding credibility isn't the same kind of tightening as a Fed hike — and it can feed a reflexive loop where the Fed holds because markets tightened, and markets tighten because the Fed held.
items.angle: Watch 30Y yields and breakevens for confirmation the market is pricing policy-credibility risk, not just rate expectations.
items.tweetA: Warsh: 'no soft inflation target, five years of above-target inflation can't be erased by nine weeks of data.' Also Warsh: holds rates while three members wanted to hike, and leans on the 30Y selloff to do the tightening for him. That's not conviction, that's hoping the market does the job so the Fed doesn't have to own the decision.
items.tweetB: The dangerous version of this story isn't inflation — it's the loop. Higher long yields hit duration-sensitive stocks, stocks fall without the usual bond hedge, deleveraging tightens conditions further, which gives the Fed another reason to wait. Every input reinforces the last one.

items.title: The next AI chokepoint isn't the GPU — it's the fiber-optic connector inside the rack
items.idea: The FCC is reportedly preparing a possible ban on Chinese optical transceiver imports, the hardware that moves data across fiber inside data centers. China's Zhongji Innolight controls roughly 27% of that market, and US players like Coherent and Lumentum don't yet have the scale to replace it. Optical names (Lumentum, Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics) rallied on the news.
items.angle: The AI arms race just moved one layer deeper than chips — into routers, transceivers and connectors — which is a much longer list of choke points than the market is pricing.
items.tweetA: Nobody's watching this line item, but it might matter more than the next GPU export rule: FCC is eyeing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers, the parts that physically move data inside AI data centers. China's Zhongji Innolight has ~27% of that market and the US has no scale replacement yet. $COHR $LITE $AAOI
items.tweetB: The AI supply chain fight quietly expanded from 'who has the best chips' to 'who controls the fiber connector.' That's a much longer, much less visible list of potential choke points — and a much longer list of future trade fights nobody's pricing yet.

items.title: Only ~25-30% of firms actually respond to the JOLTS survey — and it's probably a healthy-business skew
items.idea: Samuel Tombs notes only about 25% of firms agree to participate when the BLS asks for JOLTS data, and only ~30% respond in time for the first estimate — meaning only relatively healthy businesses are likely to opt in. LinkUp and Indeed's real-time job-posting data, by contrast, show openings slightly deteriorating this year even as headline JOLTS shows improvement.
items.angle: If JOLTS is structurally biased toward healthy respondents, the labor market could be softer than the openings-to-unemployed ratio the Fed is watching implies.
items.tweetA: JOLTS response rate is ~25-30%. Only healthy firms bother answering. Meanwhile LinkUp and Indeed — actual real-time job-posting data — show openings quietly deteriorating this year while JOLTS shows improvement. Which one should the Fed actually be reading?
items.tweetB: There's a selection-bias trade hiding in the labor data: struggling firms don't answer BLS surveys, so JOLTS structurally overstates labor demand health. If the private trackers are right and JOLTS is wrong, the 'resilient labor market' narrative propping up this rally has a crack in it.

items.title: Fidelity's Timmer: gold is underpriced relative to where global liquidity says it should trade
items.idea: Jurrien Timmer notes global money supply is rising again, and based on both the level and rate of change of global liquidity, his model implies gold could be worth more than its current trading range.
items.angle: A clean, trackable divergence: either gold catches up to the liquidity model, or global money-supply growth stalls — both are trade-relevant outcomes.
items.tweetA: Fidelity's Timmer says global liquidity (level + rate of change) implies gold should be trading above where it currently is. If that gap doesn't close via gold going up, it closes via liquidity growth stalling — which is its own signal about what central banks do next.
items.tweetB: Everyone frames gold as a Fed-cuts trade or a de-dollarization trade. Timmer's framing it as a pure global-M2 trade, full stop. Three different theses, three different macro triggers to watch for the same position.

charts.desc: Timmer's gold-vs-global-liquidity model chart — the divergence is the whole thesis in one image.

items.title: Buyback eligibility jumps from 45% to 85% of the S&P in the next two weeks
items.idea: Citadel's Scott Rubner estimates only ~45% of the S&P 500 by weight is currently eligible to repurchase shares due to earnings blackout windows, rising to 75% by end of next week and ~85% by mid-August as those windows expire — a mechanical corporate demand wave arriving exactly as retail/hedge fund positioning has been flushed clean.
items.angle: This is a scheduled, near-certain flow catalyst stacking on top of the short-covering rally — one flow handing off to the next just as the first one runs out of shorts to squeeze.
items.tweetA: Corporate buyback eligibility goes from 45% of the S&P500 to 85% in two weeks as blackout windows lift. That's a mechanical bid arriving right as the short-covering rally that got us to record highs starts running out of shorts to squeeze.
items.tweetB: The bull case nobody needs a Fed pivot or an AI breakthrough for: buyback windows reopening into a market that already de-risked in July. That's plumbing, not a narrative — and plumbing doesn't care about your macro view.

charts.desc: Rubner's chart of % of S&P500 buyback-eligible over time — the ramp from 45% to 85% is the whole story.

items.title: Dow at fresh ATHs, above rising 50-day and 200-day moving averages
items.idea: The Daily Number's Grant Hawkridge makes the simple point that fresh all-time highs are bullish, not bearish — the Dow's breakout is confirmed by a rising 50-day and 200-day moving average underneath it.
items.angle: Worth pairing with the breadth/margin data elsewhere in this window — trend confirmation plus broad participation is a harder setup to short than the 'euphoria at the top' framing implies.
items.tweetA: 'New highs are bearish, everyone's euphoric' is the take that sounds smart and is wrong most of the time. Dow's at an ATH above a rising 50-day and 200-day — that's trend confirmation, not euphoria. Fade this framework at your own cost.
items.tweetB: The permabear playbook says sell the ATH. The base rate says the opposite: fresh highs above rising 50/200-day averages have historically preceded more highs far more often than reversals. Boring, but that's what the data says.

charts.desc: Dow price chart vs 50/200-day moving averages.

items.title: Margin expansion is a 10-of-11-sector story, not just a Big Tech story
items.idea: SocGen's Manish Kabra notes profit margin expansion is happening across 10 of 11 S&P sectors right now, not just in AI-heavy Tech.
items.angle: This undercuts the 'this rally is just 7 AI stocks with accounting tailwinds' bear case — broad margin expansion is a structurally different, harder-to-short signal than concentrated mega-cap margin gains.
items.tweetA: The bear case has been 'margins are only expanding because of AI capex accounting tricks at 5 mega-caps.' SocGen's data says 10 of 11 S&P sectors are expanding margins right now. That's not a Big Tech story, that's an economy-wide pricing-power story.
items.tweetB: If margin expansion is broad rather than concentrated, the 'this rally is just 7 stocks' narrative needs an update. Broad margins plus broad participation (equal-weight S&P also ripping) is a much harder setup to short than people think.

charts.desc: SocGen chart: margin expansion breadth across 11 sectors.

items.title: SpaceX's AI segment burned $15.8B of capex to generate $2.6B of revenue in one quarter
items.idea: SpaceX's first post-IPO earnings: $7.8B Q2 revenue (+92% YoY), but shares fell as much as 8% anyway. AI segment revenue hit ~$2.6B while consuming $15.8B of capex — 86% of the company's total capital spend. The quarter also included a $540M bitcoin mark-to-market loss and $329M of related-party Tesla Megapack purchases, with the Aug 6 lockup (up to 911.5M shares) turning the print into a liquidity event.
items.angle: This is the clearest public-market illustration yet of the AI capex-to-revenue ratio the market is about to start pricing across every 'AI infrastructure' story, not just SpaceX.
items.tweetA: SpaceX's AI segment did $2.6B of revenue and burned through $15.8B of capex to do it — 86% of the whole company's capital spend for $2.6B of revenue. That ratio is about to get priced across every 'AI infrastructure' stock, not just this one.
items.tweetB: $7.8B revenue, +92% YoY, beat estimates — stock still fell 8%. The market didn't punish the growth, it punished the fact that growth now sits on a quarterly cadence next to a $329M related-party Tesla purchase and a $540M bitcoin loss. Public markets don't do vibes the way private rounds did.

charts.desc: Charts inside — worth opening (full dashboard at whatsthelatest.ai).

items.title: S&P crossed 7,700 for the first time — fueled by a retail capitulation, not just a Hormuz headline
items.idea: Qatar-brokered Hormuz de-escalation talk sent oil sharply lower and equities to record highs Tuesday (S&P above 7,700 first time, SOX on pace for best 4-day run since the 2020 COVID bottom). Strategists tie the move to positioning: last week was the biggest week of retail equity selling since 2022, creating room for a squeeze once the macro backdrop turned.
items.angle: The 'retail capitulation created the fuel' framing is the more durable read than the Hormuz headline itself, since Iran-talk headlines have failed to stick before.
items.tweetA: S&P above 7,700 for the first time, SOX on its best 4-day run since the COVID bottom — and the actual fuel wasn't the Hormuz headline, it was that retail investors had just finished their biggest selling week since 2022. Good news alone doesn't cause a melt-up. Good news landing on a market that already de-risked does.
items.tweetB: Quiet stat buried in today's wrap: quits rose the most in a year in June JOLTS while layoffs stayed flat. That's a better soft-landing signal than the S&P hitting a record, because workers only quit voluntarily when they're confident about finding the next job.

items.title: SpaceX's Thursday unlock is bigger than its entire current public float
items.idea: Up to 911.5 million SpaceX shares become eligible for sale on the Aug 6 lockup expiration — more than the current tradable float. Short interest has already risen to more than 219 million shares (~34% of tradable float) at 95% utilization, meaning almost every lendable share is already being used.
items.angle: This is a pure market-microstructure setup independent of earnings quality — a supply event bigger than the float itself, hitting a stock already down sharply from its IPO peak.
items.tweetA: 911.5 million SpaceX shares unlock Thursday. That's bigger than the entire current public float. Short interest is already 219M shares at 95% utilization — nearly every share that CAN be borrowed already is. This is a liquidity math problem, not an earnings problem.
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating whether SpaceX's AI pivot justifies the valuation. The more immediate question: what happens to price discovery when tradable supply roughly doubles in 48 hours and the shorts are already maxed out on borrow? That's market microstructure, not fundamentals.

items.title: 275 data center projects have been rejected or restricted in the US this year
items.idea: Robert Bryce reports 2026 US data center project rejections have hit 275, arguing that legacy media coverage of the local backlash against data centers 'misses the mark.'
items.angle: A real supply-side constraint on the AI buildout that's driven by local politics rather than chips or power — a bottleneck that doesn't show up in any semiconductor or grid-capacity chart.
items.tweetA: 275 data center rejections in the US this year. Everyone's modeling the AI buildout as constrained by chips and power. Increasingly it's constrained by county zoning boards and local backlash — a bottleneck that doesn't show up in any supply chain chart.
items.tweetB: The AI capex story has three bottlenecks now: chips, power, and local political will. Only the first two get modeled by Wall Street. 275 rejected data center projects says the third one might be the binding constraint sooner than people think.

charts.desc: Charts inside — worth opening (Robert Bryce's full post).

items.title: Every AI-industrial-policy skeptic should have to answer for GPS
items.idea: Matt Stoller's essay frames GPS as arguably the most successful government-owned enterprise ever — a 50-year-old system that Google Maps, Uber and huge swaths of Wall Street trading infrastructure run on top of for free.
items.angle: A ready-made historical precedent for any argument about whether government can build foundational infrastructure that private trillion-dollar businesses later monetize — worth having in the AI-industrial-policy debate.
items.tweetA: GPS is a 50-year-old government-owned system that multiple trillion-dollar companies (Uber, Google Maps) run on top of for free. Every time someone argues government can't build foundational AI infrastructure, GPS is the counterexample sitting in everyone's pocket.
items.tweetB: If you want the historical precedent for 'government builds unglamorous infrastructure, private sector builds trillion-dollar businesses on top of it for free,' it's not the internet, it's GPS. Worth remembering as the AI industrial-policy debate heats up.

items.title: AI adoption may be showing up as wage disinflation, not layoffs
items.idea: Ironsides Macro's July payroll preview argues technology innovation adoption (AI specifically) is leaving a disinflationary mark on the labor market via reduced churn (hiring + separations), which the firm ties to labor productivity. Churn is 'low churn, slow burn' — no longer deteriorating but not healthy. June's report showed a sharp divergence between the establishment and household surveys and a notable drop in labor force participation.
items.angle: If AI's labor-market fingerprint is showing up as suppressed churn and flat wages rather than headline layoffs, that's a much quieter and harder-to-see transmission mechanism than the 'AI replaces jobs' story everyone's watching for.
items.tweetA: The AI-jobs story everyone's watching for is mass layoffs. The one actually happening might be quieter: AI adoption suppressing wage growth by reducing job-to-job churn, workers not quitting for better offers because the leverage has shifted. That doesn't make a layoff headline. It shows up as flat wage growth nobody notices for two years.
items.tweetB: Two disinflationary forces are hitting labor supply at once right now: AI adoption and the reversal of the Biden-era immigration boom, pulling in opposite directions. Untangling which one is driving 'low churn, slow burn' wage growth is the real Fed debate for the next year, not the headline payroll number.

items.title: Nasdaq's 4th straight 1%+ day: only 17 of these streaks exist in history
items.idea: The Nasdaq closed with its fourth straight 1%+ daily gain — Bespoke counts only 17 other such streaks in Nasdaq history, the most recent coming in April 2025 during the post-tariff-tantrum rebound.
items.angle: A rare-event framing worth pairing with forward-return history — the setup (a post-liquidation snapback) rhymes closely with April 2025.
items.tweetA: Only 17 times in Nasdaq history has it strung together four straight 1%+ gains. The last one was the April 2025 tariff-tantrum rebound. If the pattern rhymes, the question isn't whether this melt-up is real, it's whether it's the first leg or the whole move.
items.tweetB: Four 1%+ Nasdaq days in a row is rare enough that it's basically always a liquidation-unwind signature, not a fundamentals signature. The trade isn't 'is the rally justified,' it's 'how much of the unwind is left to run.'

charts.desc: Chart plotting all 17 historical 4-day 1%+ Nasdaq streaks on a long-term price chart.

items.title: Vol is rising WITH the market — that's the FOMO tell, not the fear tell
items.idea: Normally implied volatility falls when equities rally because demand for downside protection drops. This week vol rose alongside the rally because investors are aggressively buying upside calls; put-call skew collapsed as traders paid up to avoid missing the move rather than paying up to hedge it.
items.angle: A cleaner, more actionable 'how late is this rally' signal than price action alone — spot-up/vol-up configurations historically mark late-stage chase phases.
items.tweetA: Vol is rising WITH the market right now. That's backwards — normally a rally kills implied vol because nobody wants to pay for protection. When vol rises alongside spot, people are paying up for calls, not puts. That's not confidence, that's FOMO with a chart pattern.
items.tweetB: Put-call skew just collapsed during a 5-day melt-up. Historically that's not a 'smart money is calm' signal, it's a 'everyone's chasing upside and nobody's hedging' signal, exactly the setup that makes the next 5% pullback violent instead of orderly.

items.title: "The market went from GTFO to full FOMO in four days" — a vol trader's read on the melt-up
items.idea: July's forced de-risking (hedge funds cutting exposure, leveraged ETF flushes, crowded AI trades unwound) created the launchpad for this week's rally: once oil fell and yields followed, cleaner positioning plus short covering fueled one of the largest 4-day squeezes since late 2025. The piece explicitly separates the 'roadmap' (structurally higher, supported by falling oil and easier conditions) from the 'speed limit' (the pace of the move, which is not sustainable).
items.angle: Five sessions from one-month lows to record highs means most of the visible 'return' here is a positioning unwind, not new information.
items.tweetA: 'The market went from GTFO to full FOMO in four days' — an actual quote from a vol trader this week, and it describes this rally better than any Fed or oil narrative does. This is a positioning unwind wearing a macro-catalyst costume.
items.tweetB: Five sessions from one-month lows to record highs. The fundamentals (falling oil, lower yields, decent earnings) support higher. The SPEED doesn't. When the move outruns the news by this much, the real question isn't 'is it justified,' it's 'who's left to buy the next dip before it becomes the next squeeze.'

items.title: The White House is classifying the actual test for its new AI framework
items.idea: The White House is finalizing its AI regulatory framework today and classifying the benchmarking process and coverage thresholds that decide which models get restricted. Nvidia assembled roughly 40 companies (including OpenAI and Google) opposing restrictions on using Chinese open-source models; Anthropic notably did not sign, instead arguing for more regulation on cybersecurity/safety/China grounds.
items.angle: A secret compliance bar is a structural moat for whoever can afford to guess right — and Anthropic breaking from the Nvidia-led industry coalition is the AI industry's first real visible policy fault line.
items.tweetA: The new White House AI framework's actual test, the benchmark thresholds that decide which models get restricted, is being classified. A secret compliance bar is a bar only labs with enough lawyers and lobbyists can afford to aim at. That's a moat dressed up as a safety measure.
items.tweetB: Forty companies signed Nvidia's coalition against restricting Chinese open-source AI models, OpenAI and Google included. Anthropic didn't sign, and is instead the one arguing for MORE regulation on China/safety grounds. That's the AI industry's first real policy fault line, and it's not open-source vs. closed, it's who trusts the government's judgment on China.

items.title: OpenAI hired 400+ people from Apple — now one of them is a defendant in a trade secrets suit
items.idea: Apple filed a trade secrets lawsuit against two individuals now at OpenAI's Jony Ive-led hardware unit; OpenAI has hired 400+ people from Apple in recent months, including a 24-year Apple veteran named in the suit. Both companies are trading public accusations, with the litigation playing out partly as public-opinion warfare ahead of OpenAI's anticipated mega-IPO.
items.angle: Read the timing, not the merits — OpenAI needs a clean public narrative well before its IPO, which is exactly why this is being litigated in press releases as much as in court.
items.tweetA: OpenAI has hired 400+ people from Apple for its Jony Ive hardware unit, one of them a 24-year Apple veteran now named in a trade secrets suit. The lawsuit will take years to resolve, but OpenAI needs the public narrative clean well before its IPO, which is exactly why this is being litigated in press releases as much as in court.
items.tweetB: This isn't really a trade secrets case, it's a proxy fight for who controls the AI-hardware narrative before OpenAI goes public. Watch what Apple actually ships in September (a Siri AI overhaul, a 25-year company veteran as new CEO) more than what either side says in their filings, that's the real signal.

items.title: SpaceX bought $140M of Cybertrucks Tesla couldn't sell — right before its own IPO
items.idea: Merger speculation between SpaceX and Tesla is resurfacing; the rationale is largely governance, Elon has far more control via supervoting stock at SpaceX than at Tesla, so a merger would likely fold Tesla into SpaceX's structure. SpaceX's valuation has fallen from a $2.8T IPO peak to roughly $1.5T, now close to Tesla's ~$1.3T. Notably, SpaceX bought ~$140M of Tesla Cybertrucks that Tesla couldn't otherwise sell, just before its own IPO.
items.angle: The Cybertruck purchase is the tell: related-party flows between Elon's entities happen regardless of whether a formal merger occurs, and valuation convergence between the two companies may be what actually triggers a deal, not strategy.
items.tweetA: SpaceX bought $140M of Cybertrucks Tesla couldn't sell, right before its own IPO. Whether or not a formal Tesla-SpaceX merger ever happens, the two companies are already functionally merged through related-party purchases like this one. The merger question is a governance formality at this point, not an operational one.
items.tweetB: SpaceX's valuation round-tripped from $2.8T to $1.5T, now within spitting distance of Tesla's $1.3T. A merger that would've been absurd at $2.8T (why fold your bigger, faster-growing asset into your smaller one) suddenly pencils a lot more cleanly at $1.5T. Valuation convergence, not strategy, might be what actually triggers this.

items.angle: Thin on substance, but worth logging as a positioning/sentiment data point, paid timing services touting fresh high-water marks is itself a signal.
items.tweetA: A timing-based SPX overlay strategy is claiming a fresh high-water mark with a 6.15% edge over the index. No methodology disclosed in the free tier, the number is the whole pitch. File under 'claims to verify, not claims to trade off of.'
items.tweetB: Worth noting as a sentiment data point: paid timing services touting 'new high-water marks' right now is itself a signal, that's the kind of marketing that proliferates near local market tops, when everyone's story is working.

items.title: S&P Tech sector +5% in one session on Amazon and Palantir earnings — ahead of AMD's own print
items.idea: All major US indexes rose ~2% Tuesday with the Nasdaq near +3% and the S&P 500 Tech sector up over 5% in a single day, driven by Amazon and Palantir earnings. AMD reported after the close as the next test, more than doubling YTD, with analysts betting it can repeat its CPU-market playbook (where it overtook Intel) in AI accelerators.
items.angle: The CPU-to-AI-leadership parallel for AMD is worth stress-testing, Intel lost on execution, but Nvidia's moat is CUDA software lock-in, a fundamentally different wall to climb than x86 competition ever was.
items.tweetA: AMD's whole 2026 bull case in one sentence: it did to Intel in CPUs what it's trying to do to Nvidia in AI accelerators. The problem is the two situations aren't the same trade, Intel lost on execution, Nvidia's moat is CUDA software lock-in, a completely different kind of wall to climb.
items.tweetB: S&P Tech +5% in a single session on Amazon and Palantir earnings alone, ahead of AMD's print. When a sector moves 5% in a day on OTHER companies' earnings, that's not stock-picking, that's a beta unwind, AMD's print barely needs to be good, it just needs to not break the narrative.

items.title: Three prop trading firms now have $100B of combined equity capital — more balance sheet than most G-SIBs
items.idea: Jane Street, Citadel Securities and Hudson River Trading together generate more than $65B of annual revenue with a combined equity capital base of roughly $100B, part of an industry-wide 'the big get bigger' consolidation among roughly 13 elite professional trading firms (including Optiver, IMC, Virtu, XTX, Jump, DRW).
items.angle: The same scale-begets-scale dynamic reshaping AI infrastructure is playing out in market-making, worth tracking as a parallel case study in how concentrated an industry gets once balance sheet becomes the moat.
items.tweetA: Jane Street, Citadel Securities and Hudson River Trading: $65B+ combined revenue, ~$100B combined equity capital. Three firms now have the balance sheet of a G-SIB bank without any of the regulatory capital requirements of one. That asymmetry is the real story, not who's winning market share.
items.tweetB: Market making is following the exact same 'big gets bigger, scale is the only moat' pattern as AI infrastructure right now, a handful of firms with balance sheet size dominate distribution and talent, and everyone else becomes an acquisition target instead of a competitor.

items.title: Jane Street's revenue lead over Flow Traders went from 10x to 73x in five years — Flow Traders is now a takeover target
items.idea: Flow Traders' revenue gap to Jane Street widened from 10x in 2020 to 73x in 2025; its European ETF market share fell from 35-40% to ~25%. Flow Traders trades near book value (€970m equity, ~€1.2bn market cap) at 7-8x 2026E earnings. Rupak Ghose argues the most likely outcome is acquisition by fellow Amsterdam prop shop Optiver or IMC Trading, both of which could easily afford it.
items.angle: A concrete, numbers-backed takeover thesis worth tracking for M&A optionality, not a turnaround story.
items.tweetA: Jane Street's revenue lead over Flow Traders went from 10x to 73x in five years. That's not a competitive gap anymore, that's a different industry. Flow Traders trading near book value at 7-8x 2026 earnings makes it a cheap option on Optiver or IMC Trading finally pulling the trigger on a takeover. €1.2bn market cap, easily affordable for either.
items.tweetB: The Flow Traders story is what happens when 'we do too many things, most not very well' meets a market structure where scale is now the only moat that matters. Sympathetic new CEO, right diagnosis, probably too late, the more interesting trade is who buys the carcass, not whether the turnaround works.

charts.desc: Table comparing Flow Traders' revenue/profit trend vs. Optiver, IMC Trading and Jane Street.
